title: Results — provisional
text:
Headline findings

Macaque is the closest model to human BBB. 96.8% nucleotide identity at the coding-sequence level. For almost every gene, macaque sits above the diagonal — more similar to human than mouse.
Mouse is more divergent (84.1%) but still highly conserved. Mouse models remain biologically defensible, but ~16% sequence divergence is present. Where mouse and human BBB phenotypes differ clinically, this divergence is one possible explanation.
BBB genes are under stronger purifying selection than liver genes — most visibly in the human-macaque comparison (BBB dN/dS 0.152 vs Liver 0.196, p < 10⁻⁶ after Bonferroni correction). The signal is weaker in human-mouse because at ~80 million years, all genes have accumulated extensive change.
Gene duplication produces dramatic divergence. Paralogous mouse genes (e.g. Abcb1a + Abcb1b for human ABCB1) are only ~47% identical to human, vs ~85% for one-to-one orthologues. Effect size is large (rank-biserial r = 0.72).
Conservation and human BBB expression are independent. A gene’s validation score (0–3 datasets) does not predict how conserved it is at the sequence level.

title: Results — provisional
text:
Biological interpretation
Strong purifying selection on BBB genes makes biological sense. The BBB controls what enters and exits the brain — broken transporters or tight junctions would let toxins in or block essential nutrients. Evolution actively removes protein-changing mutations from these genes, more aggressively than for liver genes.
The fact that this signal is most visible in the human-macaque comparison — not human-mouse — reflects evolutionary timescale. Subtle differential selection is detectable when species are close enough that not all genes have saturated their substitutions. At ~80 million years for human-mouse, this signal is lost in the noise.

title: Results — provisional
text:
Findings, re-graded against the audit
The five findings above are stated as originally written. This is what the audit does to each of them.

  1. Macaque is the closest model to human BBB Direction holds, number unreliable
  As stated: 96.8% nucleotide identity; macaque sits above the diagonal for almost every gene.
  % identity was computed in step5c and never recomputed after the codon-aware fix. 224 one-to-one macaque pairs score under 85%, which is biologically impossible — SLC2A1 comes out at 71.4%. That is the longest-transcript heuristic comparing non-corresponding isoforms. Macaque being closer to human than mouse is safe; the figure 96.8% is not.



  2. Mouse is more divergent (84.1%) but still highly conserved Number unreliable
  As stated: ~16% sequence divergence; mouse models remain biologically defensible.
  The same % identity problem, plus the gene list itself is wrong. This figure describes a set that is largely pericyte and developmental-timing genes, not BBB-enriched ones. The claim is not disproven — it has not yet been tested on the right genes.



  3. BBB genes are under stronger purifying selection than liver genes Withdrawn
  As stated: BBB dN/dS 0.152 vs liver 0.196, p < 10⁻⁶ after Bonferroni correction.
  The comparator is not a liver control. 86.6% of it is brain-expressed, with brain and liver medians effectively identical (31.3 vs 31.2). It is a housekeeping set — and housekeeping genes are unusually conserved — so the test compared BBB genes against one of the most conserved groups in the genome and read the result as tissue-specific selection. The statistics are correct; the contrast is not. This claim cannot be made until the control is rebuilt, and step 5d's asymmetric orthologue rule has to be fixed at the same time.



  4. Gene duplication produces dramatic divergence Survives
  As stated: paralogous mouse genes ~47% identical vs ~85% for one-to-one orthologues; rank-biserial r = 0.72.
  This is a contrast within the BBB set, so it does not depend on the liver control, and the effect is far too large to be an artefact of the % identity problem. It is the strongest surviving result in the project — worth stating plainly, because a page about mistakes that reports nothing left standing is its own kind of distortion.



  5. Conservation and human BBB expression are independent Uninformative
  As stated: a gene's 0–3 validation score does not predict how conserved it is.
  The validation score barely carries information. One of its three components read only Yang's arterial sheet; another asked whether a gene was detected at all, which 88.5% of genes pass — and that component alone is why 1,131 of 1,526 genes score exactly 1. A null result against a near-constant variable says nothing in either direction.

text:
Limitations

What counts as a canonical BBB gene was never pinned down
The project uses the phrase “canonical BBB genes” without ever saying which genes it means. The working definition is the one the field uses: genes consistently identified across multiple independent transcriptomic studies as highly expressed and functionally important in brain endothelial cells. “Canonical” does not mean the only important BBB genes, it means the well validated ones.
Four papers read for the literature review do name them, so the master list of 1,526 genes can be checked against those names.

Two different reasons for absence, which should not be conflated. PECAM1, KDR and CDH5 are general endothelial markers expressed in endothelium everywhere. An enrichment-based list is supposed to exclude them, and their absence is correct.
CLDN5 and TJP1 are excluded by the same rule, because they too are expressed in all endothelia, but here the rule removes the machinery that makes the barrier a barrier. The clearest illustration is the claudin family: of 1,526 genes, the only claudin present is CLDN6, which is not a BBB claudin.
The transporters are better covered. The list contains 52 SLC genes, about 3.4% of it, and 9 ABC transporters, including all the ones the literature names.
What this means for every result on this page. Enrichment and importance are not the same thing, and this list selects for the first. Any statement here about “BBB genes” should be read as genes differentially enriched in brain endothelium in two mouse studies, not genes that make the barrier work. The tight junction proteins, which are the barrier, are almost entirely missing.
The fix is to name the canonical set explicitly, check membership, and either state that the enrichment rule excludes some of them or carry them as a named supplementary set that is scored alongside. This is separate from the three fixes and does not depend on them.


Methodological caveats

Pairwise dN/dS, not phylogenetic. A more rigorous analysis uses PAML codeml on a multi-species alignment with an explicit phylogenetic tree.
Longest-transcript heuristic. MANE Select / Ensembl Canonical (step5b_alt_canonical_transcripts.R) are more standard. The canonical FASTAs are already generated.
Multiple testing correction was applied to primary tests only. Stratified subgroup analyses (by Daneman filter, validation score, paralogue type) are exploratory.



Biological caveats

The starting gene list is enrichment-based. See the section below, which sets out what that excludes.
Liver is one specific control choice. A different control (brain non-BBB genes, genes matched by protein domain) could give a different picture.
Coding sequence only. Regulatory regions (promoters, enhancers, UTRs) — where most cross-species expression-level differences live — were deliberately excluded.

title: Barrier against brain disease, by Daniela Kaufer and Alon Friedman
text:
Back to the issue notes
Listed online as “Damage to a protective shield around the brain may lead to Alzheimer’s”, originally published May 2021.
Topic. What happens to the brain once the blood brain barrier starts to leak, and whether the damage that follows can be reversed. This was a very interesting paper to read.
Where it started. These two researchers came across Gulf War syndrome, where they found that pyridostigmine was reaching the brain when it was not supposed to. Soldiers were reporting long term tiredness and similar symptoms, and they believed the penetration of the blood brain barrier by pyridostigmine was the primary factor.
What they were speculating at the time is that stress would make the blood brain barrier leaky, allowing proteins that are normally not found past it to appear.
Their first experiments: they let mice swim in water to put them under a lot of stress, then injected blue dye into their veins. They found that these brains had a strong blue tint. So one of the first assumptions was that putting animals, or even people, under a lot of stress would cause the blood brain barrier to leak. They published these results in Nature Medicine.
The link to brain disease. Barrier damage in patients with some brain disorders does seem to point to Alzheimer’s patients, who seem to have a leaky blood brain barrier.
What they wanted to see was the brain function directly after the blood brain barrier started to malfunction, meaning once it gets leaky. They gave rats a chemical that poked holes in their barrier, then dissected their brains at various later times.
The storm. What they found was what they call a social media storm, as an analogy. There was a trigger in the blood brain barrier which suddenly allowed epilepsy like signals to appear, very suddenly. This storm happened only after they mimicked a blood brain barrier leak. They repeated it several times and it worked.
Then they injected blood into the rat’s brain, and came to the conclusion that specifically albumin is responsible for this reaction. They were not thrilled with this catch, because albumin is in the blood and the blood fulfils a lot of different tasks in our body. So before running the experiments again, they tried to understand what albumin does in the blood brain barrier context.
The mechanism, as I understand it. When albumin contacts an astrocyte it binds on TGF beta. TGF beta is an indicator for inflammation, or can cause inflammation, and when you have inflammation cytokines are released. On the other hand, TGF beta also activates the astrocyte and the microglia.
Albumin provides a positive feedback loop and an overproduction of TGF beta. So there is an over-activation of astrocytes and microglia, which in turn activates more TGF beta, which in turn causes more inflammation and cytokines. This is essentially the stress they had recorded in mice previously, which also made the blood brain barrier leaky.
They also say that astrocytes become senescent, that is, chemically active even after their role in the feedback loop is done.
Age. They compared albumin concentrations in the brain depending on the age of mice, and found that albumin in younger mice was not apparent, but started to show up when they were in middle age. They checked this for humans and it seems to be the same case: heightened albumin levels accompanied greater amounts of TGF beta in astrocytes, and also in people who had neurological diseases.
Correlation or causation. This is where it gets interesting. They infused albumin into the intact healthy brains of young mice for one week, and these brains started to work and function like older brains, with abnormal neuronal function.
To make sure the experiment was not flawed by TGF beta, they cut out the TGF beta cascade that came after the leak, so that you are really seeing a causation result. It turned out that the mice with the receptors and with albumin in their brains had a lot of trouble getting out of the water maze, while the young mice without the TGF beta cascade behaved in a very normal way and found their way out.
The drug. You cannot knock out TGF beta in humans, that is too risky. Instead they were contacted by a medical startup drug company, and were given a drug called IPW, which is an inhibitor for the activity of TGF beta.
They gave the mice the IPW drug, and it turned out that these mice, even though they had had abnormal functions for a very long time, were able to regain their brain functions to the state they were in before albumin was injected. So it seems like the brain is able to rebound from some types of abnormal activity.
What this changed for me. When I think about diseases like Alzheimer’s, I think the damage done to the brain is permanent, and that when a brain deteriorates it is not possible to get it back to a state where it functions normally, even if you had a magical drug that cancelled out the negative effects.
It turns out it is possible. The brain has some hidden feedback loop, some kind of mechanism that allows it to regain normal function, to such an extent that even the researchers were quite surprised, because the mice that were injected with albumin and then got the IPW drug were able to swim out of the maze.
Worth confirming from the printed copy. The exact drug designation and the name of the company that supplied it. IPW is most likely IPW-5371, a TGF beta receptor inhibitor.

title: Pipeline & Methods
text:
Step 1 — Gene List

Breaks results step1_extract_BBB_genelist.R — wrong source tables.
Three of the four Daneman tables read here are the wrong tables. S3 is Daneman’s pericyte-specific list, not core BBB genes; S4 and S5 are developmentally up- and down-regulated CNS vascular genes, not the brain-vs-liver and brain-vs-lung contrasts assumed below. S6 — the real BBB-enriched table — was never opened. A further 92 genes were lost silently to toupper() and to HomoloGene’s 2014 gene names.
The 1-gene overlap with Munji flagged below was the correct alarm and the wrong diagnosis: S3 was not too restrictive, it was the pericyte table. Using S6 gives 151 of 411 genes overlapping Munji. Full entry in the Audit tab.


Why did we do Step 1?
Before we can measure anything, we need to know which genes to measure. The BBB does not have one official gene list — different research groups have profiled brain endothelial cells at different times using different technologies. Step 1 builds a single, well-annotated master list from the two most-cited published datasets, tags each gene by how stringently it was identified, and converts mouse gene symbols to human ones so the whole pipeline can work in human gene space.






NoteData flow



Full script: scripts/step1_extract_BBB_genelist.R Reads: raw_data/daneman_2010/Daneman2010_S3/S4/S5_*.xls, raw_data/munji_2019/Munji2019_S5_*.xlsx Writes: processed/master_BBB_genelist.csv Packages: readxl, dplyr, readr, homologene




Why Daneman + Munji
Two foundational papers each profiled brain endothelial cells in mouse:

Daneman et al. 2010 — compared brain ECs to peripheral, liver, and lung ECs (supplementary tables S3, S4, S5). The S3 list is the strictest (genes enriched vs both liver AND lung).
Munji et al. 2019 — top CNS endothelial-enriched genes (supplementary table S5).

Mouse gene symbols from both papers were converted to human HGNC symbols using the homologene R package. Each gene was tagged by source paper and which Daneman filter it passed (liver_and_lung, liver_only, or lung_only).


Why we expanded to S3+S4+S5
Initial work used only the strict S3 list (~545 genes). Canonical BBB genes like SLC2A1 (GLUT1, the main brain glucose transporter) were missing — S3 demands enrichment vs liver AND lung simultaneously, and SLC2A1 is also expressed in liver endothelium. Including S4 and S5 with stringency tags captured these missing genes while preserving the ability to filter back to S3 for sensitivity analysis.

Steps 3 & 3b — Mapping

92 genes lost step3_map_ensembl_crossspecies.R — inherited breakage.
The 92 gene names broken in step 1 return nothing from BioMart and drop out of every downstream calculation with no error raised. The step itself is doing what it was asked.


Overstated fix step3b_biomart_orthology_confidence.R — recovers nothing.
The script header says it recovers the genes step 1 dropped. It does not: it re-queries the same out-of-date names and recovers none of the 92. This is also where 196 one-to-many pairs enter the BBB set at only 25.8% protein identity — pairs that step 5d then excludes from the control set but not from the BBB set.


Circular check step3c_biotype_check.R — cannot fail.
A CDS FASTA contains only protein-coding genes by definition, so a non-coding gene has no entry, comes back blank, and blank was not counted as a failure. The reassuring “all protein-coding, no annotation gap” result below was guaranteed by the method, not earned by it. 250 rows have no macaque label at all and were invisible to the check.


Naming Execution order does not match the step names.
step4b writes master_BBB_genelist_validated.csv, which step3b reads. The true order is 1 → 2 → 3 → 4b → 3b → 3c → 4c → 5a…, so step 4b runs before step 3b despite the numbering. The Audit tab’s register lists the real run order.


Why did we do Steps 3 & 3b?
To compare DNA sequences across species, we need a stable, species-specific identifier for each gene — not the gene symbol (which changes between species, e.g. human SLC2A1 vs mouse Slc2a1), but a permanent database ID. Ensembl gene IDs (ENSG... for human, ENSMUSG... for mouse, ENSMMUG... for macaque) serve this purpose. This step also retrieves orthologue relationships: which mouse gene corresponds to which human gene, and whether it is a clean one-to-one match or a more complex one-to-many (gene duplication) case. That distinction matters a lot for interpreting conservation scores.

text:
Steps 4b & 4c — Validation

Two reading bugs step4b_human_validation.R — the score means less than it looks.
Yang S6 was read without naming a sheet, so only the first of seven sheets loaded. That column really means “is an arterial marker” — 36 hits — and the capillary sheet, the most BBB-relevant one, was never opened. Wälchli’s test was “expression above zero in any cell type”, which 88.5% of all genes pass; that single component is why 1,131 of 1,526 genes score exactly 1. Winkler’s parse is correct.
Consequence: Human_BBB_Datasets_N is close to a constant, so any result stratified on it — including “conservation and human BBB expression are independent” — is uninformative rather than negative.


Breaks results step4c_liver_control_geneset.R — the brain filter never ran.
The filter looked for a tissue called "brain". The Human Protein Atlas has no such label — it lists regions: cerebral cortex, hippocampal formation, cerebellum. Zero rows matched, the missing values became zeros, and everything passed. The tell is sitting in the saved file: every Brain_nTPM value is exactly 0.0.
Recomputed properly, 86.6% of the “liver control” genes are also expressed in brain, and their median brain expression (31.3) matches their median liver expression (31.2). This is not a liver control — it is a general housekeeping set, and housekeeping genes are among the most conserved in the genome, which biases every BBB-vs-control comparison in a known direction.


Why did we do Steps 4b & 4c?
Two separate questions are answered here:
Step 4b — The gene list comes from mouse studies, but we are ultimately interested in the human BBB. Before running thousands of alignments, we want to flag which genes have cross-species expression evidence in human brain endothelium (using three independent human EC datasets). This does not remove any genes — it gives each gene a confidence score (0–3) that can be used for sensitivity analysis later.
Step 4c — The core scientific question is whether BBB genes are unusually conserved, not just conserved. To answer that, we need something to compare against. A liver control set provides a biologically meaningful baseline: liver is a highly expressed, well-studied tissue, so if BBB genes are more conserved than liver genes, that difference is real and not just a property of all expressed genes.






WarningWhat went wrong — and why Step 4 was removed



Step 4 downloaded full GTF genome annotation files (~1.5 GB per species, ×3 = ~4.5 GB total) with the intention of extracting CDS coordinates manually. After downloading all three we found that Ensembl already provides pre-extracted CDS FASTA files (~20 MB per species) — the same information at a fraction of the size. Step 4 was removed entirely, which is why the numbering jumps from Step 3b to Step 4b.

text:
Steps 5a-b — CDS

Clean step5a_download_cds_fastas.R — Ensembl 113, all three species.


Rough heuristic step5b_extract_cds_sequences.R — longest ≠ equivalent.
Taking the longest isoform means human and mouse can land on non-corresponding versions of the same gene, which makes them look more different than they are. This is the origin of the 224 impossible macaque scores that appear in step 5c.
step5b_alt_canonical_transcripts.R implements the standard alternative — MANE Select / Ensembl Canonical — and the canonical FASTAs already sit in genomes/. It was written and never switched in.


Why did we do Steps 5a-b?
Conservation analysis works at the DNA sequence level — we need the actual nucleotide letters for each gene in each species. The full genome of a mammal is ~3 billion base pairs, but most of that is non-coding (introns, regulatory regions, intergenic space). We only want the coding sequence (CDS) — the stretch of DNA that actually gets translated into protein. Ensembl provides pre-extracted CDS files for every annotated transcript, which are ~150× smaller than the full genome files and much faster to work with. Step 5b then extracts just the CDS sequences for our specific BBB and liver gene lists, ready for alignment.






NoteData flow



Full scripts: scripts/step5a_download_cds_fastas.R, scripts/step5b_extract_cds_sequences.R Step 5a downloads Ensembl CDS FASTAs → genomes/*.cds.all.fa.gz (×3 species) Step 5b reads: genome FASTAs + gene lists → Writes: genomes/cds_BBB_*.fa and genomes/cds_liver_*.fa (×3 species each) Packages: Biostrings, dplyr, readr Note: genomes/ is excluded from git (too large). Run Step 5a to populate it before Step 5b.




What we did
Ensembl provides pre-extracted CDS FASTA files for every annotated transcript. For each gene with multiple transcripts (alternative splicing), we kept the longest CDS as a heuristic for the full open reading frame.

Alternative: scripts/step5b_alt_canonical_transcripts.R uses Ensembl Canonical / MANE Select transcripts instead — one curated transcript per gene, jointly designated by NCBI + EMBL-EBI. The FASTAs are already generated in genomes/cds_canonical_*.fa.

title: Pipeline & Methods
text:
Steps 5c-d — Scoring

Partly superseded step5c_align_and_score.R — dN/dS fixed later, % identity never was.
dN/dS here was computed on sequences that were trimmed but never actually aligned. That is genuinely wrong, and it is correctly fixed in step 5f. But the % identity was never recomputed, so every identity figure in the results still comes from this step.
Two numbers show the size of the problem. 38% of genes came out with dS pinned at the 10.0 ceiling — saturated nonsense — which falls to 2% after the codon-aware fix. And 224 one-to-one macaque pairs score under 85%, with SLC2A1 at 71.4% where macaque should sit near 97%. That is step 5b’s longest-transcript heuristic picking non-corresponding isoforms, then PID1 dividing by the longer alignment and reporting the length difference as evolutionary distance.


Breaks results step5d_liver_scoring.R — the two sides were scored under different rules.
Described as “the same measurements”, but the control set kept only the single best-matching orthologue per gene while the BBB set kept every match, including the 196 one-to-many pairs at 25.8% identity admitted in step 3b. The BBB group was carrying dead weight the control group was not.
That alone reverses the headline direction: as published, BBB 84.12 vs liver 84.32 (BBB looks less conserved); under one rule for both sides, BBB 85.04 vs liver 84.47 (BBB is more conserved).


Why did we do Steps 5c-d?
This is the core of the project — the step that actually measures conservation. For each BBB gene (and each liver control gene), we align its coding sequence between species and compute two numbers: how similar the DNA letters are (% identity), and whether evolution is actively protecting the gene from protein-changing mutations (dN/dS). Running this for both BBB genes and liver genes separately sets up the statistical comparison in Step 5e: are BBB genes more conserved than a typical expressed gene?






NoteData flow



Full scripts: scripts/step5c_align_and_score.R (BBB), scripts/step5d_liver_scoring.R (liver) Reads: genomes/cds_BBB_*.fa or genomes/cds_liver_*.fa, processed/master_BBB_genelist_complete.csv Writes: processed/conservation_scores_BBB.csv, processed/conservation_scores_liver.csv, processed/conservation_scores_combined.csv Packages: Biostrings, pwalign, seqinr, dplyr, readr Note: Step 5c takes 20–40 min (~1,500 alignments). Step 5d takes 60–90 min (~3,000 alignments).




Pairwise global alignment
For each gene we ran a Needleman-Wunsch global alignment between species pairs, then computed % identity and dN/dS:
aln <- pwalign::pairwiseAlignment(
  seq1, seq2, type = "global",
  substitutionMatrix = nucleotideSubstitutionMatrix(match=1, mismatch=-1),
  gapOpening = -5, gapExtension = -2
)
pct_identity <- pwalign::pid(aln, type = "PID1")
# PID1 = matches / alignment_length (including gaps)
Why global, not local? These are orthologous genes — they should align end-to-end. Local alignment would only find the most similar segment, over-estimating similarity for genes that diverge at the edges.


Why % identity AND dN/dS

% identity — how similar are the letters, simple and interpretable
dN/dS — how often do mutations change the protein (non-synonymous, dN) vs leave it unchanged (synonymous, dS). dN/dS << 1 means evolution is removing protein-changing mutations (purifying selection).

title: Pipeline & Methods
text:
Steps 5e-g — Statistics

Clean step5e_statistics.R, step5f_recompute_dnds.R, step5g_stats_v2.R — all three correct.
The statistical framework is sound: the right tests for non-normal data, correctly corrected, with subgroup analyses honestly labelled exploratory. Step 5f is the project’s one real fix — the codon-aware recomputation moved one-to-many mouse dN/dS from 0.14 to 0.354 and dropped saturated dS from 38% of genes to 2%.
What is wrong is what went into these tests: the gene list from step 1, the control set from step 4c, and the asymmetric orthologue rule from step 5d. Step 5f’s only gap is scope — it fixed dN/dS and left % identity untouched.


Why did we do Steps 5e-g?
Having conservation scores for ~4,500 gene pairs is not enough on its own — we need to know whether the differences between BBB and liver genes are statistically meaningful or just random variation. Step 5e runs the formal tests. Steps 5f and 5g were added specifically because the initial dN/dS values were wrong (see the bug callout below): Step 5f recomputes them correctly using a codon-aware alignment pipeline, and Step 5g re-runs the statistics on the corrected values with proper multiple testing correction applied.






NoteData flow



Full scripts: scripts/step5e_statistics.R, scripts/step5f_recompute_dnds.R, scripts/step5g_stats_v2.R Step 5e reads conservation_scores_combined.csv → writes conservation_summary.txt Step 5f reads combined scores + CDS FASTAs → writes conservation_scores_combined_v2.csv Step 5g reads v2 scores → writes conservation_summary_v2.txt Packages: Biostrings, pwalign, seqinr, dplyr, readr




Step 5e: First-pass statistics
Wilcoxon rank-sum tests comparing BBB vs liver (non-parametric, because % identity is bounded and skewed). Stratified analyses by Daneman filter, validation score, and orthologue type.


Step 5f: dN/dS recomputation






WarningWhat went wrong — three separate dN/dS bugs



Bug 1 — all NA values: The ape package (loaded alongside seqinr) has its own kaks() function and silently overrode seqinr::kaks(). Fix: explicit namespace.
Bug 2 — values inflated: seqinr::kaks() assumes codon-aligned input — same length, same reading frame positions in both sequences. We were passing unaligned sequences, inflating the non-synonymous count. Especially large effect for human vs mouse (~80 million year divergence).
Bug 3 — wrong translation function: dplyr’s translate() (an SQL function) was silently overriding Biostrings::translate(). Fix: Biostrings::translate(DNAString(seq), if.fuzzy.codon = "X").


The fix: translate both sequences to amino acids → align proteins with BLOSUM62 → back-map codons using protein alignment → strip gap columns → pass codon-aligned pair to seqinr::kaks():
aa1 <- Biostrings::translate(DNAString(nt1), if.fuzzy.codon = "X")
aa2 <- Biostrings::translate(DNAString(nt2), if.fuzzy.codon = "X")
protein_aln <- pwalign::pairwiseAlignment(aa1, aa2, type = "global",
                 substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62",
                 gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 4)
# back-map to codons, strip gaps, run seqinr::kaks()
# full implementation: scripts/step5f_recompute_dnds.R


Step 5g: Multiple testing correction
Bonferroni and FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg) applied to the four primary BBB-vs-liver comparisons. Stratified tests are flagged as exploratory.

title: Park et al. 2019
text:
My reading
The model they used was a blood brain barrier chip, in which they generated the blood brain barrier under hypoxic conditions, and they differentiated the brain-like microvascular endothelial cells under hypoxic conditions as well.
Why hypoxia. The blood brain barrier establishes itself under hypoxic conditions in the first place. In the embryo it forms in a low oxygen environment. So if you can replicate the original differentiation state of these pluripotent stem cells, the likelihood is higher that you achieve the barrier phenotype you are after. That is why hypoxia was used, and they explain it in the first paragraph.
For the regions of the brain, they tried to replicate the blood brain barrier itself, including its tight junctions, transporter proteins, astrocytes and pericytes.
What they measured was the osmotic opening. They did two experiments with the blood brain barrier in which they looked at whether they can administer FDA approved cancer drugs, which they were able to do. They also compared their findings with the research literature for in vivo studies in animals and in humans, but they focus more on humans.
Statistics and modelling. What they did was more like trying out the blood brain barrier and seeing how it performs, because it is an artificially generated one. They talk about the duration of the model, which is one week, and how it can be used.
There are two case studies in which they use osmotic opening to look at whether they can administer an FDA approved drug, which they were able to do.
They also assess P-gp activity in the BBB chip by treating the chips with P-gp inhibitors, and they used MS analysis to measure the permeability of citalopram. So there is a connection between P-gp and citalopram.
They also analysed the activities of BCRP and MRP1, where they measured the influx of rhodamine 123 and DiOC2 into the CNS channel. So broadly, you could say they administered different inhibitors to the BBB chip to see what goes through into the CNS and what does not, and whether it works as known in the literature or not.
Then they administered doxorubicin to study brain transporter dependent drug efflux, which worked.
They also recapitulated BBB shuttling activities on chip with Angiopep-2. Angiopep-2 has been used with multiple drugs including paclitaxel and a cancer therapeutic HER2 antibody, which I think is used in breast cancer. They found that Angiopep-2 had a 3.5 fold greater capacity to penetrate into the CNS compared with Q-dots, which was the standard control.
Then they talked about how they were able to open the blood brain barrier on chip and how it regained complete function after about four hours following osmotic opening, in which they used osmotic solutions.
At the end, they are essentially saying that if you want to create these versatile and quite good models of the BBB chip, you either lower oxygen levels or add HIF1α inducing mimetics, in order to enable differentiation of endothelial cells that recapitulate human relevant physiological blood brain barrier properties when the cells interface with human brain astrocytes and pericytes in a two channel microfluidic BBB chip.
They also show that the microfluidics played a part, or were more relevant, for being able to deliver a clinically approved therapeutic, to do an osmotic opening, and to showcase clinically relevant functionalities.

title: Park et al. 2019
text:
What I take from it
What I felt the focus of this paper was: that you can actually build these BBB chips, and you can test them and try out physiologically well documented processes, and simply showcase that this is possible.
That also answers the regional identity question. Since it is a model, regional identity was not in focus.
The two most important things they did:

They recapitulated the in vivo interaction of P-gp and citalopram under physiological flow, which could not be reproduced under static conditions in past 3D models. So they are showcasing the advantage of microfluidic systems here, to mimic in vivo cellular transport.
They showed that in vivo shuttling of CNS targeting peptides, nanoparticles and antibodies across the BBB was recapitulated using the enhanced BBB chip, enabling examination of CNS targeting drug delivery systems as well.

Their overall goal is to advance personalised medicine by building more physiologically and clinically relevant BBB chips that can hold longer, differentiate more, and show more abilities than what they have currently shown.

title: Park et al. 2019
text:
Checks against the paper
Small corrections and additions from reading the text alongside the notes.

Paclitaxel and the HER2 antibody are cited background, not experiments in this paper. The paper says the brain-penetrating capacity of multiple drugs, including paclitaxel and a cancer therapeutic HER2 antibody, has been shown to be enhanced when modified with Angiopep-2, citing earlier work. What Park’s group actually tested was Angiopep-2-coated quantum dot nanoparticles, 20 nm, against Q-dots coated with a scrambled peptide. The 3.5 fold figure is theirs.
The HER2 antibody guess is right. A therapeutic HER2 antibody is trastuzumab, used in HER2-positive breast cancer.
The FDA approved drug in the osmotic opening experiment is cetuximab, an anti-EGFR therapeutic antibody, flowed alongside a 10 kDa dextran tracer. The paper calls this, to their knowledge, the first demonstration of delivery of a clinically approved antibody drug across the human BBB in vitro by reversible osmotic opening.
Recovery timing. TEER dropped by about 50% within 2 h of hypertonic mannitol, and both the dextran and the antibody permeability returned to the normal range within 4 h of switching back to isotonic medium. The experiment runs to 4.5 h in total.
Duration. One week is right for the hypoxia-differentiated chip. With CoCl2 instead of hypoxia, barrier function was sustained for more than two weeks.
Doxorubicin numbers. Inhibiting P-gp with verapamil produced a 2.7 fold increase in doxorubicin influx into the CNS channel. Inhibiting MRP1 or BCRP did not change it, so P-gp is the pump doing the work for this drug.
One experiment not in the notes: they also tested two anti-transferrin-receptor antibodies, MEM75 and 13E4, and got about threefold higher penetration of MEM75, which matches what had been predicted in vitro but never reproduced in a human BBB model. This is a second shuttling mechanism alongside Angiopep-2 and LRP1.
Barrier tightness. The chips reached about 25,000 Ω, roughly two orders of magnitude above BBB chips made with primary human BMVECs at around 400 Ω.

title: Park et al. 2019
text:
Open questions from this read

MEM75 and 13E4 differ by pH-dependent binding affinity to the transferrin receptor. Worth understanding properly if antibody shuttling comes up again.

title: Park et al. 2019
section: How it relates to this project
text:
How it relates to this project
This is the most different paper in the review so far. It has no cross-species comparison, no sequence, and no conservation measure. Its relevance is indirect but real.

It is an argument against the pipeline this project is premised on. The opening frame of this project is mouse, then macaque, then human, and the question of whether sequence conservation makes that chain trustworthy. Park’s work attacks the same problem from the other end: build a human system in vitro and skip the species jump entirely. The paper states plainly that neither animal models nor existing in vitro cultures effectively mimic the human BBB. If human chips mature, cross-species conservation becomes less load-bearing as a translational argument, and more of a question about evolutionary biology. Worth saying somewhere in the project’s framing.
It independently nominates several genes on this project’s list as functionally important, and does so by function rather than by expression: P-gp (ABCB1), BCRP (ABCG2), MRP1 and MRP4, GLUT-1 (SLC2A1), plus LRP1 and the transferrin receptor as shuttling routes. These are not just detected here, they are shown to pump, and knocking each one out with a specific inhibitor changes what crosses.
Claudin-5 again, and this time it matters. Park treats claudin-5 as a defining marker of a working barrier. This project’s gene list does not contain CLDN5, because it failed the differential-expression cutoff in the source studies: it is expressed in all endothelia, not only brain. That is a defensible reason for a enrichment-based list, but it means the list omits a gene the functional literature treats as central. See the limitations.
It connects directly to Kumabe 2025 on in vitro model fidelity. Kumabe found claudin-5 absent from hCMEC/D3, an immortalised line, and found immortalised lines drifting towards generic vein endothelium. Park’s chip does express claudin-5 and reaches barrier values two orders of magnitude above primary-cell chips. Read together, the two papers say the same thing from opposite directions: how the endothelium is produced determines whether an in vitro BBB is a BBB at all.
Function is not presence. step4b scores a gene on whether it was detected in human datasets. Park’s whole method rests on the difference between a transporter being present and a transporter working. That is a fair challenge to how this project’s validation score is constructed, quite apart from the parsing bugs the audit records.

title: Park et al. 2019
text:
Reference detail from the paper

Chip: 2-channel PDMS microfluidic device, porous PET membrane (2 µm pores) coated with collagen IV and fibronectin. Astrocytes and pericytes seeded 7:3 on the apical side, iPS-BMVECs on the vascular side. Flow at 100 µL/h giving 6 dyne/cm² shear, medium viscosity 3 to 4 cP.
Differentiation: iPSCs under 5% O2 from D0, retinoic acid at D6 to D8, seeded on chip at D9, then shifted to normoxia. Hypoxia raised mRNA for VE-cadherin, PECAM-1, GLUT-1, INSR, P-gp, BCRP, MRP1 and MRP4, and Wnt7a by over 25-fold.
Barrier: impedance about 25,000 Ω under hypoxia differentiation against about 400 Ω for chips with primary human BMVECs. Papp about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁹ cm/s, inversely correlated with tracer size.
Efflux selectivity: verapamil (P-gp) raised rhodamine 123 and DiOC2 in the CNS channel; Ko143 (BCRP) affected DiOC2 but not rhodamine 123; MK571 (MRP1) affected rhodamine 123 only. Doxorubicin rose 2.7-fold with verapamil and was unchanged by MK571 or Ko143.
Citalopram: permeability increased when P-gp was inhibited in the chip, matching in vivo animal studies. The paper notes that past in vitro BBB models failed to identify citalopram as a P-gp substrate, and the equivalent Transwell experiment showed no such effect.
Osmotic opening: 485 mOsmol/L mannitol for 1 h. TEER fell about 50% within 2 h. 10 kDa dextran Papp rose from 3 to 32 × 10⁻⁸ cm/s and cetuximab from 2 to 5.1 × 10⁻⁸ cm/s. Both back to normal within 4 h.
Shuttling: Angiopep-2-conjugated Q-dots showed about 3.5-fold greater CNS penetration than scrambled-peptide Q-dots, with no change in barrier integrity. Anti-TfR MEM75 showed about threefold higher penetration than 13E4.

title: Miao et al. 2026
text: Miao Y, Wang J, Li W, Mäe MA, Jeansson M, Muhl L, He L (2026). Distinct gene expression profiles in blood-brain barrier capillary endothelial cells between mice and humans. Microvascular Research 166:104933. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mvr.2026.104933. Open access under CC BY 4.0.

title: Miao et al. 2026
text:
My reading
This was a very fitting paper. At the very beginning they just talk about what they are doing, and their objective was to compare the transcriptomic profile of blood brain barrier capillary endothelial cells between adult mice and humans.
What they found is that 169 genes were consistently enriched in human BBB capillary endothelial cells compared to mouse, whereas 386 genes were enriched in mouse compared to human. They have some species specific genes that were expressed in just one or the other.
What they conclude is that there is broad conservation, but that the distinct transcriptomic differences between human and mouse BBB capillary endothelial cells need to be taken seriously. At the very end they also talk about how this is applicable to the drug development process.
Introduction. First they introduce the function of endothelial cells, and how other people have tried to understand the transcriptomic profile. Turns out that bulk RNA is limited due to the lack of cellular resolution. I am not quite sure exactly what they mean here, but maybe it is the missing data. Only with the emergence of single cell RNA sequencing and single nucleus RNA sequencing have they been able to do a much more precise characterisation of barrier cell types.
Materials and methods. Specifically I had to look out for what method they were using: are they referring to single nucleus RNA sequencing or single cell RNA sequencing. These were things I needed to watch for.
They also talk about their manual inspection to remove a small number of contaminating cells. They removed cells with pericyte marker expression, and also immune cell markers.
Then they looked at the human snRNA-seq and scRNA-seq data. They talk about their patient age and so on.
Data integration and comparison is pretty solid, because we did something similar. They used one-to-one orthologous gene pairs. They used R with the Seurat package, which we also used. Then they applied the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which we also used, and a Bonferroni adjusted p-value, which we also used.
Results. They again talk about having analysed the transcriptomic profile of mouse and human. It turns out that specifically the markers CLDN5 and FLT1 were the most abundantly expressed transcripts. They also look at novel markers such as MFSD2A, KDR and TFRC, and they find the gene abundance profiles were highly correlated across platforms.
Then they look at the human BBB endothelial transcriptome again, and check that the canonical markers of capillary endothelial cells were consistently recovered in both datasets, which makes their case pretty strong.
Then they looked at the mouse and human BBB endothelial transcriptomes together. They checked the markers, saw that both were expressed in both datasets, and that is when they showed the species specific enrichment.
Then they point out that the SLC transporter family was specifically expressed, in that a substantial number of the differentially expressed genes belong to this family.
Then they talk about the validation, which they did using ISH images and immunohistochemistry.
Discussion. They discuss that the transcriptomic profile has some similarities but is not fully defined, and that when you do drug development you need to watch out specifically for the different enriched genes in the BBB capillary endothelial cell profile between mouse and human.

title: Miao et al. 2026
text:
What I take from it
They used the same comparison machinery we did: one-to-one orthologues, Seurat, Wilcoxon, Bonferroni. Seeing our own choices turn up in a 2026 paper in the field is reassuring about the statistics, whatever else is wrong upstream.

title: Miao et al. 2026
text:
Checks against the paper

On bulk RNA and cellular resolution. Bulk RNA-seq grinds up the whole tissue and measures the average across every cell in it. Brain tissue is overwhelmingly neurons and glia, so the endothelial signal is a small fraction of the total and cannot be separated out. It is not missing data so much as blended data. Single cell and single nucleus methods measure one cell at a time, so capillary endothelial cells can be picked out and compared directly. This is the same problem noted for Wälchli in Kumabe.
Both methods are used, on both species. Mouse is scRNA-seq on two platforms. Human is one snRNA-seq dataset (Allen Brain Atlas, Smart-seq) and one scRNA-seq dataset (10x).
The human tissue is worth noting. The post-mortem dataset is three individuals, mean age 49, mean post-mortem interval 22.7 h, yielding only 51 capillary endothelial cells. The surgical dataset is peritumoral tissue adjacent to gliomas from seven patients. Neither is healthy brain in the way the mouse tissue is, which is a real limit on the comparison and one the paper does not dwell on.
A small internal inconsistency. The abstract and results say 386 genes enriched in mouse; the discussion says 385. Worth knowing which to quote.
The numbers behind the claim. Cross-platform correlation within mouse was Pearson r = 0.941. Between species the correlation was r = 0.68. 15,675 one-to-one orthologous pairs went into the comparison.

title: Miao et al. 2026
text:
The species-specific genes it names
Higher or specific in mouse: Slco1c1, Slc22a8, Pglyrp1, Tspan13, Ucp2. Slco1c1 encodes Oatp1c1, which carries thyroid hormone T4 across the mouse barrier.
Higher or specific in human: A2M, CLEC3B, BTNL9, SPOCK3, RUNDC3B. A2M is alpha-2-macroglobulin, a protease inhibitor implicated in amyloid-beta clearance.
Conserved and robust in both: FLT1, CLDN5, PECAM1, SLC2A1 (GLUT1), with MFSD2A and CLDN5 consistently recovered as canonical capillary markers.

title: Miao et al. 2026
section: How it relates to this project
text:
How it relates to this project

This is the closest paper yet to what the project is doing, and it is two months old. Same two species, same question of how far mouse stands in for human at the barrier, and published while this project was running. The difference is the measurement: they compare expression, this project compares coding sequence. That is a real distinction and it is worth stating in the project’s framing rather than discovering later.
It validates the statistical choices. One-to-one orthologues, Seurat, Wilcoxon rank-sum, Bonferroni adjustment. That is the same framework as step5e and step5g. The audit already found the statistics to be the clean part of the pipeline; this is independent confirmation that they match current practice in the field.
It settles the one-to-many orthologue question. They restricted to one-to-one orthologous pairs only, 15,675 of them, and cross-checked Ensembl against NCBI. This project admitted 196 one-to-many pairs at 25.8% identity into the BBB set in step3b, and then step5d excluded them from the control but not from the BBB set. The field standard is to use one-to-one throughout. That is direct support for the step5d fix.
The sharpest finding for this project: the divergent family is the SLC family. A substantial proportion of the differentially expressed genes are solute carriers. This project’s gene list carries 52 SLC genes, about 3.4% of it, including the ones named here, and it is measuring how conserved their sequence is. Miao shows that this is exactly the family whose expression diverges most between mouse and human. So the two measurements may well disagree, with a gene conserved in sequence and expressed quite differently. That is not a problem with either study. It is the most interesting thing either could say, and it is a result this project is positioned to contribute to.
CLDN5 for the fourth time. Here it is one of the two most abundantly expressed transcripts in mouse BBB capillary endothelial cells, and a canonical marker robustly expressed in both species. It is still absent from this project’s gene list because it failed an enrichment cutoff. Four independent papers now treat it as central. This needs writing into the limitations.
It gives a ready-made comparison set. The 169 human-enriched and 386 mouse-enriched genes are a published, thresholded list of where the two species differ at the barrier. Once this project’s conservation scores are corrected, asking whether those divergent genes are also less conserved in sequence is a direct, cheap and genuinely novel question.

title: Literature Review
text: Papers are read against six fields, in the order below, so entries stay comparable. Each paper has its own page — the card links through. Terms are collected in the Methods Glossary; the papers the pipeline itself is built on are cited on the Resources page.

title: Literature Review
text:
How each paper is read

1. Year published

Establishes what was technically possible at the time. A 2010 microarray study and a 2025 deep-proteomics study are not making the same kind of claim.

2. Model(s) used

Which species, whether the comparison is within or across species, and whether the cross-species claim rests on the same tissue.

3. Brain region

Recorded whenever stated. Cerebrovascular endothelium differs between brain regions, and between arterial, capillary and venous segments of the same vessel tree, so a gene “BBB-enriched” in one region or segment may not be in another. Where a paper does not state the region — or where regions are not matched between species — that is recorded too.

4. What is measured

DNA, RNA, or protein. Sequence conservation and expression answer different questions, and a paper measuring RNA cannot on its own support a claim about conservation.

5. How it is measured

Microarray, bulk RNA-seq, single-cell/nucleus RNA-seq, proteomics, genomic sequencing. For RNA-seq, bulk or single-cell, and whether cells were sorted. Bulk brain tissue drowns endothelial signal in neurons; isolated microvessels or sorted endothelium do not.

6. Statistical and modelling techniques

What was done to compare across species — orthologue assignment, differential tests and thresholds, alignment, selection estimates, phylogenetic versus pairwise, multiple-testing correction.

title: Literature Review
text:
Papers


Song et al. 2020

2020 Human · mouse RNA Laser capture microdissection

Brain microvessels cut straight out of frozen tissue by laser, so low abundance transcripts survive and nothing is dissociated. The transporter families are the story: Slco1c1 and Slc22a8 mouse-enriched, SLCO1A2 human-only, and a worked example of a species difference in one transporter breaking a mouse disease model. Also a first molecular definition of human brain pericytes.
Read the entry →


Miao et al. 2026

2026 Mouse · human RNA Single-cell and single-nucleus

The closest paper yet to what this project is doing, published two months ago. Same two species and the same question of how far mouse stands in for human at the barrier, but measured through expression rather than coding sequence. 169 genes enriched in human capillary endothelium, 386 in mouse, and the family that diverges most is the SLC transporters, a block this project’s gene list carries 52 of.
Read the entry →


O’Brown et al. 2018

2018 Fly · shark · zebrafish · mouse · human Review Comparative

A comparative review of the barrier across organisms, from Ehrlich’s dye experiments to iPSC models, with zebrafish and mouse compared in detail. It makes this project’s central claim, that barrier machinery is conserved across species, from expression and function rather than sequence. It also reports regional differences in permeability within the mouse brain, and states that barrier properties are acquired from the neural microenvironment rather than being intrinsic to the endothelial cell.
Read the entry →


Park et al. 2019

2019 Human only, in vitro Barrier function Organ-on-a-chip

A human blood brain barrier built on a two channel microfluidic chip, from iPSC-derived endothelium differentiated under hypoxia and interfaced with primary human astrocytes and pericytes. It holds barrier function for a week, shows working efflux pumps rather than merely present ones, and delivers a clinically approved antibody across the barrier by reversible osmotic opening. No cross-species comparison at all, which is the point: it is an attempt to skip the species jump entirely.
Read the entry →


Kumabe et al. 2025

2025 Human · cynomolgus monkey · mouse Protein DIA proteomics

Deep proteomic profiling of brain microvessels isolated from all three species, alongside five cultured BBB model cell types. Clustering puts human closest to monkey and mouse furthest out — the same ordering this project finds in coding sequence, reached from protein expression instead. Also the primate BBB expression data the pipeline currently lacks, and a clear demonstration that immortalised cell lines drift away from real brain endothelium.
Read the entry →

title: Methods Glossary
text:
Every entry says which paper it was first met in, so a term can be traced back to the reading that prompted it.

Immortalised cells

A cell line engineered to divide indefinitely, usually by inserting a gene such as SV40 T antigen or telomerase. Ordinary primary cells taken from tissue divide a limited number of times and then stop, which makes them awkward to work with; immortalised lines are convenient, reproducible and cheap. The cost is that they drift away from the original tissue — which is precisely what Kumabe measures: hCMEC/D3 and HBMEC/ciβ resemble generic vein endothelium (HUVEC) more than they resemble real brain microvessels, and hCMEC/D3 has lost claudin-5 entirely.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

Western blot

A method to check whether one specific protein is present, and roughly how much. Proteins are separated by size in a gel, transferred onto a membrane, and probed with an antibody that binds only the target. Here it is a quality control, not a result: claudin-5 present in the microvessel fraction shows the fraction contains endothelium; PSD95 absent shows it is not contaminated with neurons. β-actin is the loading control — it should be equal in every lane, confirming equal amounts of protein were loaded.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

DIA — data-independent acquisition

A mass-spectrometry strategy. In the older data-dependent approach the instrument picks the most intense peptides to fragment and measure, so weakly abundant proteins are missed and different runs measure different things. DIA fragments everything in successive mass windows, so the same proteins are measured in every run. That is why this study can compare across species and samples with confidence, and why it reaches 7,000–8,000 proteins.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

QTAP — quantitative targeted absolute proteomics

Instead of relative abundance, this measures the actual molar amount of a chosen protein, by spiking in a synthetic version of one of its peptides labelled with heavy isotopes. The known standard and the real peptide behave identically but differ in mass, so the ratio gives an absolute concentration. Used here to confirm the SLC43A3 result independently of DIA.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

BCA assay (bicinchoninic acid)

A colour-change assay for total protein concentration in a sample. Used so that equal amounts of protein go into each analysis.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

Two-tailed Student’s t-test

Tests whether the means of two groups differ. “Two-tailed” means it tests for a difference in either direction — higher or lower — rather than predicting the direction in advance. Two-tailed is the conservative default.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

One-way ANOVA

The extension of the t-test to three or more groups, with “one-way” meaning the groups differ along a single factor — here, species. It answers only “are these groups all the same?”, not which pair differs. Running repeated t-tests between every pair instead would inflate the false-positive rate, which is the problem ANOVA exists to avoid.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

Tukey post-hoc test

Run after a significant ANOVA to find which pairs actually differ, while correcting for the fact that you are making several comparisons at once.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment

A multiple-testing correction. Testing thousands of proteins at p < 0.05 produces many false positives by chance alone. BH controls the false discovery rate — the expected proportion of claimed hits that are wrong — and is less severe than Bonferroni, which is why it suits large screens. The corrected value is the “adjusted p-value”. This project uses both, in step5g.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

PCA — principal component analysis

Compresses thousands of measurements per sample into a few axes that capture most of the variation, so samples can be plotted and compared. When human and monkey sit near each other on PC1 and mouse sits apart, that is a statement about overall proteome similarity.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

Hierarchical clustering

Repeatedly joins the two most similar samples until everything is in one tree. The branching order and branch heights show which samples group together and how strongly — independent confirmation of what the PCA shows.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

GO enrichment analysis

Gene Ontology assigns standard functional labels to genes and proteins. Enrichment asks whether a list contains more of a given label than chance would give — here, showing that BMV-enriched proteins are disproportionately “transmembrane transporter activity” and “maintenance of blood-brain barrier”. DAVID is the tool that performs this test.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

TPM — transcripts per million

A normalised unit of RNA-seq expression, adjusted for both sequencing depth and transcript length so values can be compared between genes and samples.
First met in Kumabe et al. 2025.

Organ-on-a-chip

A small device, usually moulded in silicone, with hollow channels lined by living human cells and fluid flowing through them. The point is to reproduce the mechanical conditions of a tissue, flow, shear and a two-sided interface, which a flat dish cannot. In a BBB chip the endothelium lines one channel, brain cells sit in the other, and a porous membrane between them is the barrier being measured.
First met in Park et al. 2019.

iPSC, induced pluripotent stem cell

An adult cell, often a skin or blood cell, reprogrammed back into a stem-cell-like state from which it can be pushed to become almost any cell type. It gives an unlimited supply of human cells of a chosen type. The catch is that the result is a cell differentiated towards a type rather than one taken from tissue, so how well it matches the real thing has to be demonstrated, not assumed.
First met in Park et al. 2019.

TEER, transendothelial electrical resistance

A measure of how tight a cell barrier is, taken by passing a small current across it. A leaky layer conducts easily and reads low; a well-sealed layer with intact tight junctions resists and reads high. It is the standard quick check that a barrier model is behaving like a barrier, and it can be watched over days without disturbing the cells.
First met in Park et al. 2019.

Apparent permeability (Papp)

How fast a given molecule crosses the barrier, in cm/s. Measured by putting a tracer on one side and sampling the other. Unlike TEER, it is molecule-specific, so it can show that a barrier is tight to one compound and open to another, which is what makes it useful for testing transporters.
First met in Park et al. 2019.

Efflux pump

A transporter that actively pushes molecules out of a cell, using energy. At the BBB the major ones, P-gp (ABCB1), BCRP (ABCG2) and the MRPs, sit on the blood-facing surface of the endothelium and pump drugs back into the bloodstream. They are a large part of why so few drugs reach the brain. Their activity is demonstrated by blocking them with a specific inhibitor and showing that more of the drug then crosses.
First met in Park et al. 2019.

Transcytosis

Transport of a molecule through a cell rather than between cells: taken in on one side in a vesicle, carried across, released on the other. Large molecules such as antibodies cannot slip between tight junctions, so this is the route drug designers target, usually by attaching a ligand for a receptor the endothelium already uses, such as the transferrin receptor or LRP1.
First met in Park et al. 2019.

Hypoxia and normoxia

Low oxygen and normal oxygen. Standard cell culture runs at about 20% O2, which is far above what cells experience in a real tissue. The developing brain forms its vasculature at roughly 1 to 8% O2, which is the reasoning behind differentiating the cells at 5% O2.
First met in Park et al. 2019.

HIF1α and HIF1α mimetics

HIF1α is the transcription factor cells use to sense and respond to low oxygen. Under normal oxygen it is rapidly degraded; under hypoxia it is stabilised and switches on a programme of genes. A mimetic such as CoCl2 or DMOG stabilises HIF1α chemically, producing the hypoxic response without needing a low-oxygen incubator.
First met in Park et al. 2019.

Two-way ANOVA

ANOVA where the groups differ along two factors at once, for example species and treatment, rather than one. It tests each factor separately and also whether they interact, meaning the effect of one depends on the level of the other.
First met in Park et al. 2019.

title: Audit — what’s wrong
text:
Every defect below is pinned to the numbered script step it lives in, using the script’s own filename. The step names here and the step names in the pipeline are the same names — the ambiguity in the tab labels (which bundle several steps together) is not carried into the audit.

The count

  Breaks results3Fix these and a stated conclusion changes. Steps 1, 4c, 5d.
  Numbers move6Real defects that shift figures without reversing a claim.
  Clean6No defect in the step itself, including both hard parts.
  Open questions6Not bugs — decisions, or data the project does not have.



Register — all 15 numbered steps
Run is the order the scripts actually execute in, which is not the order the step names imply: step4b writes the file step3b reads, so 4b runs before 3b.





Step
Run
What it does · what's wrong
Verdict




step1
1
Build the master BBB gene list. Three of the four Daneman tables are the wrong tables — S3 is the pericyte-specific list (Pdgfrb, Kcnj8, Vtn, Zic1), S4 and S5 are developmentally up- and down-regulated CNS vascular genes. S6, the real BBB-enriched table, was never opened. A further 92 genes were lost silently: 18 to toupper() mangling the lowercase orf convention, 74 to HomoloGene's 2014 gene names.
Wrong sources


step2
2
Process the Wälchli Seurat object. Method correct — grouped by ECclusters rather than the default. Two things to know rather than fix: the input is gitignored so the step cannot re-run from a clean clone, and the Mitochondrial cluster (dying cells, not a cell type) is still in the output.
Clean


step3
3
Map to Ensembl IDs across three species. The 92 names broken in step 1 return nothing from BioMart and drop out of every downstream calculation with no error raised. The step is doing what it was asked; it inherits the damage.
92 genes lost


step4b
4
Cross-reference against human EC datasets. Yang S6 was read without naming a sheet, so only the first sheet loaded — the column means "is an arterial marker" (36 hits) and the capillary sheet, the most BBB-relevant one, was never opened. Wälchli's test was "expression above zero in any cell type", which 88.5% of all genes pass; that alone is why 1,131 of 1,526 genes score exactly 1. Winkler's parse is correct.
Two reading bugs


step3b
5
Add orthology confidence. The script header says it recovers the genes step 1 dropped. It does not — it re-queries the same out-of-date names and recovers none of the 92. It is also where 196 one-to-many pairs enter the BBB set at only 25.8% protein identity, which step 5d then excludes from the control set but not from the BBB set.
Overstated fix


step3c
6
Gene biotype audit. The check cannot fail. A CDS FASTA contains only protein-coding genes by definition, so a non-coding gene has no entry, comes back blank, and blank was not counted as a failure. 250 rows have no macaque label at all and were invisible to it. The reassuring answer was guaranteed by the method.
Circular check


step4c
7
Build the liver control gene set. The third filter looked for a tissue called "brain"; the Human Protein Atlas has no such label, only regions (cerebral cortex, hippocampal formation, cerebellum…). Zero rows matched, the missing values became zeros, everything passed. The tell is in the saved file: every Brain_nTPM value is exactly 0.0. Recomputed properly, 86.6% of the "liver control" is brain-expressed, median brain 31.3 against median liver 31.2. It is a housekeeping set — among the most conserved genes in the genome.
Filter never ran


step5a
8
Download CDS FASTAs. Ensembl release 113 for all three species — GRCh38, GRCm39, Mmul_10. Straight downloads, nothing to get wrong.
Clean


step5b
9
Extract one CDS per gene. Takes the longest isoform. Longest is not necessarily equivalent: human and mouse can land on non-corresponding versions of the same gene, which makes them look more different than they are. This is the origin of the 224 impossible macaque scores visible in step 5c.
Rough heuristic


step5b_alt
—
MANE Select / Ensembl Canonical transcripts. The standard alternative to the longest-isoform heuristic. It was written, it runs, and the canonical FASTAs already sit in genomes/. It was never switched in.
Written, unused


step5c
10
Align and score the BBB genes. dN/dS was computed on sequences that were trimmed but never aligned — genuinely wrong, and correctly fixed later in step 5f. But the % identity was never recomputed, so every identity figure in the results still comes from here. Two numbers show the damage: 38% of genes came out with dS pinned at the 10.0 ceiling (2% after the 5f fix), and 224 one-to-one macaque pairs score under 85% — SLC2A1 at 71.4%, which is biologically impossible.
Partly superseded


step5d
11
Score the liver control. Described as "the same measurements", but it kept only the single best-matching orthologue per gene while the BBB set kept every match including the bad ones. Different rules on the two sides of the comparison — and that alone reverses the headline direction.
Asymmetric rules


step5e
12
First-pass statistics. Wilcoxon rank-sum (correct — these data are not normal) with rank-biserial effect sizes. Superseded by 5g, but not wrong.
Clean


step5f
13
Recompute dN/dS, codon-aware. Translate to protein, align the proteins, map back onto codons, discard gapped codons, then score. This is the fix, and it mattered: one-to-many mouse dN/dS moved from 0.14 to 0.354. The only gap is scope — it fixed dN/dS and left % identity untouched.
This is the fix


step5g
14
Multiple testing correction. Bonferroni and FDR across the four primary comparisons, with subgroup analyses honestly labelled exploratory. Correct. What is wrong is what went into it — steps 1, 4c and 5d.
Clean


step5h
15
Mouse vs macaque. Same codon-aware pipeline with no human reference. No defect of its own — but it inherits the step 1 gene list, so its numbers move when step 1 is fixed.
Clean







Three fixes change the conclusions

step1 — point it at Daneman S6, drop S3/S4/S5, retire the Daneman_Filter column. Replace toupper() with a real ortholog mapping so the 92 lost genes come back.
step4c — one line, so the brain filter matches the Atlas’s real region names. Then a separate decision about what the control should actually be.
step5d — one orthologue rule applied to both groups.

Then re-run step5c through step5h. Everything else is numbers moving, not conclusions changing.


What we still need to figure out
These are not defects. They need a decision, a dataset, or both — and this is the section that grows as the literature review continues.

  
    What should the control actually be?
    Fixing the step4c filter gives a genuine liver set, but liver may not be the right comparator at all. Brain non-BBB genes, or genes matched on protein domain, would each test a different claim.
    Needs — Dr. Clelland
  
  
    Can the macaque arm rest on mouse-defined biology?
    Every gene earned its place from a mouse study. Real macaque DNA is used throughout steps 5a–5h, but no macaque study tells us which genes macaque brain vessels actually switch on. The rhesus brain single-cell atlas (Science Advances 2023, ~1M nuclei, 28 regions, on CellxGene) would close this — and widens project scope.
    Needs — a dataset and sign-off
  
  
    Should % identity be recomputed the way dN/dS was?
    Step 5f fixed dN/dS with codon-aware alignment and left identity alone. Switching step5b to MANE Select and re-running identity would likely remove the 224 impossible macaque scores. The canonical FASTAs already exist.
    Needs — a decision, then compute time
  
  
    Why did we never use Wälchli's 12 EC subtypes?
    The dataset resolves capillary from arterial from venous endothelium. Step 4b collapsed all of it to a single above-zero test. The most valuable thing about the dataset is the one thing the pipeline never asked it.
    Needs — a new analysis
  
  
    Where did Giger 2010 come from, and what replaces it?
    Logged as the macaque dataset. Its 13 samples are all human (taxid 9606) — the macaque in that paper belongs to Khaitovich et al. under a separate accession that was never downloaded. It also compares neurons to endothelium rather than brain to peripheral endothelium, so it is not a BBB gene list for any species.
    Needs — literature review
  
  
    Should step 2 be reproducible from a clean clone?
    The Seurat input is gitignored and exists on one machine. The Mitochondrial cluster is also still sitting in the output matrix.
    Needs — a housekeeping decision

text: Nothing on this page has been done yet. It is a record of what the project would need next, kept separate from the audit because these are not defects — a defect has a fix, and these need a decision, a dataset, or a method the project does not currently use.

title: Extensions
section: Before anything else — the three fixes
text:
Before anything else — the three fixes
The extensions below are only worth doing on corrected inputs. In priority order:

step1 — point it at Daneman S6, drop S3/S4/S5, retire the Daneman_Filter column, and replace toupper() with a real orthologue mapping so the 92 silently dropped genes return.
step4c — one line, so the brain filter matches the Human Protein Atlas’s real region names. Then decide what the control should actually be.
step5d — one orthologue rule applied to both groups.

Then re-run step5c through step5h.

title: Extensions
text:
Method extensions

Phylogenetic dN/dS with PAML
The current estimate is pairwise: each species pair scored independently. The rigorous approach runs codeml on a multi-species alignment with an explicit tree, which separates lineage-specific selection from shared ancestral signal and handles saturation properly. At ~80 My of human–mouse divergence, saturation is the specific worry — 38% of genes hit the dS ceiling before the codon-aware fix, and 2% still do.
Needs: PAML, a three-species alignment per gene, and considerably more compute.


MANE Select transcripts, and re-running % identity
step5b_alt_canonical_transcripts.R already generates canonical FASTAs and was never switched in. Doing so, then recomputing % identity the way step5f recomputed dN/dS, should remove the 224 one-to-one macaque pairs scoring under 85% — figures that are currently reporting isoform length mismatch as evolutionary distance.
This is the cheapest high-value extension: the code exists and the sequences are already downloaded.


Regulatory and non-coding sequence
The analysis is coding sequence only. Promoters, enhancers and UTRs were deliberately excluded — and they are where most cross-species differences in expression level are thought to live. A gene can be 95% identical in its coding sequence and regulated completely differently. Extending to regulatory regions would test whether BBB conservation at the protein level is matched by conservation in how the genes are switched on.
Needs: a definition of the regulatory region per gene, and an alignment strategy that tolerates far lower conservation than CDS.

title: Extensions
text:
Data extensions

Narrow the project to the SLC and ABC transporter families
Rather than scoring the whole enrichment-derived list, restrict to the solute carrier and ATP binding cassette families. This would fix several problems at once:

Membership stops being a judgement call. The families are defined by gene nomenclature, so the “what counts as a canonical BBB gene” problem in the limitations does not arise.
There is something to compare against. Song 2020 and Miao 2026 independently report the same transporters diverging between mouse and human, including Slco1c1, Slc22a8 and SLCO1A2. A sequence conservation result would land against a published expression result.
The question gains a consequence. These are the families that decide whether a drug crosses, which is why both papers frame their species differences as a drug development problem.
The data already exists. The gene list carries 52 SLC and 9 ABC genes.

Needs: a decision on whether narrowing the scope is acceptable, since it changes the project from “are BBB genes conserved” to “are BBB transporters conserved”. The second is a smaller claim and a much more defensible one.


A macaque expression atlas
The project’s largest structural gap. Real macaque DNA is used throughout, but no macaque study tells us which genes macaque brain vessels actually express — every gene earned its place from a mouse study, and the paper logged as the macaque dataset (Giger 2010) contains no macaque samples.
The candidate is the rhesus macaque single-nucleus brain atlas (Science Advances 2023, ~1M nuclei, 28 regions, on CellxGene).
Needs: the dataset, and Dr. Clelland’s sign-off — this widens the project’s scope.


Wälchli’s endothelial subtypes
The atlas resolves 12 endothelial subtypes; step4b collapsed all of it to one above-zero test. Asking whether a gene is capillary-specific rather than merely detected is the question this dataset exists to answer, and would turn the validation score from a near-constant into something informative.
Needs: nothing new — the matrix is already in processed/.


A better control, or several
Liver was one choice. Brain non-BBB genes would test whether the signal is specific to the barrier rather than to the brain; genes matched on protein domain would control for the fact that transporters and tight-junction proteins are structurally unusual. Running more than one control would say more than fixing the single one.
Needs: Dr. Clelland’s decision on what claim the control is meant to support.

title: Extensions
text:
Housekeeping

Make step2 reproducible from a clean clone, or document the exact supplementary file to fetch.
Drop the Mitochondrial cluster — dying cells, not a cell type — from the Wälchli output matrix.
Correct the step3c biotype check so it can actually fail, or remove it.

title: Blood–Brain Barrier Gene Conservation Across Human, Mouse, and Macaque
text:
This project has been my way of learning bioinformatics and the biology of the blood–brain barrier at the same time. It is a quantitative analysis of coding-sequence conservation and selection pressure in blood–brain barrier genes across human, mouse and macaque, using liver genes as a control group.
The site documents the whole thing: the steps I took, the materials I used, the audit I did afterwards, and what has to be fixed first before this data can be reused. The bioinformatics pipeline is a rough structure — usable, but it needs polishing. Alongside it is a literature review, currently in progress, where I will add and comment on the papers I read.
